question.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{\sqrt{2x-y}-4}{16-2x+y} & =\frac{\sqrt{2(7)-(-2)}-4}{16-2(7)+(-2)} \\  & =\frac{4-4}{16-14-2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{\sqrt{2x-y}-4}{16-2x+y} & ={lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{(\sqrt{2x-y}-4)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)}{(16-2x+y)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{2x-y-16}{(16-2x+y)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{16-2x+y}{(16-2x+y)(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{\cancel{16-2x+y}}{\cancel{(16-2x+y)}(\sqrt{2x-y}+4)} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-y}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{lim}_{x\to (7,-2)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-y}+4} & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(7)-(-2)}+4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{16}+4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4+4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{8}.$
